summary: Daniel Whitenack (Data Dan), founder/CEO of Prediction Guard and co-host of the Practical AI podcast, delivers a talk on deploying secure and accurate AI systems based on real-world enterprise experience. He scopes the discussion to open-access large language models and frames the talk as a checklist of five problems practitioners face: hallucination, supply chain vulnerabilities, flaky or vulnerable model servers, data breaches via RAG systems, and prompt injection. For hallucination, RAG grounds output but cannot detect failures and increases data breach risk. Prediction Guard uses an ensemble of fine-tuned factual consistency models (referencing UniEval and BART score) to score factual inconsistencies between AI output and ground truth data, with LLM-as-judge as an alternative. For supply chain vulnerabilities, he recommends maintaining a trusted model registry with appropriate licenses from trusted sources, using hash checks or attestation when pulling models, cloning models to your own registry, keeping Transformers' untrusted code flag false, and applying enterprise-grade endpoint monitoring, file integrity monitoring, pen tests, and SOC 2-style compliance thinking. For data breaches, he recommends placing PII and PHI detection filters in front of the LLM—configurable to block, strip, or replace PII with fake values—and leveraging confidential computing technologies like Intel SGX or TDX for memory encryption, plus trusted attestation to verify server environments before sending requests. For prompt injection, Prediction Guard uses a custom-built firewall layer with an expanding set of injection examples and ensembled classification models to detect and filter injections. In Q&A, he addresses latency by using smaller NLP models (around 200ms) instead of chained LLM-as-judge calls, and leveraging vector search for quick semantic comparisons. On pre-production testing, he notes individual prompt injection models can be called in isolation with adjustable thresholds. On data access, he describes leveraging existing RBAC in databases like PostgreSQL with PG Vector or text-to-SQL, and notes some customers use LLM-based approaches to categorize document stores before ingestion. He also recommends systems like Immuta for data lake access policy management and tool calling with proper roles. On SIEM integration, he emphasizes minimal logging (not logging prompts or completions), file integrity monitoring for model artifacts (not just code), and detecting token-based denial-of-service anomalies. On agent security, he references the LLM Top 10 vulnerability list, highlighting excessive agency as a key risk, and recommends restricting permissions and using dry-run approval patterns with human-in-the-loop review, noting that generating initial configurations is the hard part while post-editing by skilled engineers is relatively easy.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Enterprise AI adoption faces a gap between the promise of AI co-pilots and real-world deployment challenges across five risk categories
Hallucination is a high-stakes problem; RAG grounds output but cannot detect when the model fails and increases data breach risk
Prediction Guard uses an ensemble of fine-tuned factual consistency models (UniEval, BART score) to score factual inconsistencies between AI output and ground truth
Supply chain mitigations include trusted model registries, hash checks/attestation, cloning models internally, and keeping Transformers' untrusted code flag false
Data breach mitigations include configurable PII/PHI detection filters (block, strip, or replace) and confidential computing (Intel SGX/TDX) for memory encryption
Prompt injection is addressed with a custom firewall layer using ensembled classification models and an expanding set of injection examples

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.summary: Daniel Whitenack introduces himself as founder/CEO of Prediction Guard and co-host of the Practical AI podcast. He scopes the talk to open-access LLMs in enterprise contexts, sharing learnings from real-world customer deployments on risk and accuracy.

sections.title: Checklist of LLM Deployment Problems
sections.summary: Daniel builds a checklist of five problems: hallucination (with a field medic example showing high stakes), supply chain vulnerabilities via open-source model code, flaky or vulnerable model servers exposing PII, data breaches from RAG systems leaking sensitive documents, and prompt injection attacks exploiting connected systems.

sections.title: Addressing Hallucination
sections.summary: Daniel begins solutions with hallucination. RAG grounds output but introduces privacy concerns and cannot detect failures. Prediction Guard's approach uses fine-tuned factual consistency models (referencing UniEval, BART score) in an ensemble within an inference framework to score factual inconsistencies between AI output and ground truth. LLM-as-judge is mentioned as an alternative.

sections.title: Addressing Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
sections.summary: Daniel recommends maintaining a trusted model registry with appropriate commercial licenses from trusted sources, using hash checks or attestation when pulling models, and cloning models to your own registry. He advises keeping Transformers' untrusted code flag false and applying enterprise-grade server security: endpoint monitoring, file integrity monitoring, pen tests, and SOC 2-style compliance thinking, even when using third-party model hosting.

sections.title: Addressing Data Breaches
sections.summary: Daniel recommends placing PII and PHI detection filters in front of the LLM, configurable to block, strip, or replace PII with fake values. He notes that logged or unencrypted prompts remain vulnerable, advocating confidential computing technologies like Intel SGX or TDX for memory encryption and trusted attestation to verify server environments before sending requests.

sections.title: Addressing Prompt Injection
sections.summary: Daniel describes a custom-built firewall layer in front of the LLM using an expanding set of prompt injection examples and ensembled classification models to detect and filter likely injections in a configurable way. He emphasizes getting easy, known mitigations in place from the start to build trust in AI systems.

sections.title: Q&A: Latency, Testing, and Data Access
sections.summary: In Q&A, Daniel addresses latency by using smaller NLP models (~200ms) instead of chained LLM-as-judge calls (~4s for main LLM) and leveraging vector search for quick semantic comparisons. On pre-production testing, he notes prompt injection models can be called individually with adjustable thresholds for visibility. On data access, he describes leveraging existing RBAC in databases like PostgreSQL with PG Vector or text-to-SQL, and notes some customers use LLM-based approaches to categorize document stores before ingestion.

sections.title: Q&A: Data Lake Access and SIEM Integration
sections.summary: Daniel continues the data access discussion, recommending systems like Immuta for managing data lake and file store access policies, and using LLM tool calling with proper roles to interact with those APIs. On SIEM integration, he notes Prediction Guard's production system avoids logging prompts or completions. He highlights file integrity monitoring for model artifacts (data, not just code) as important for both performance and security. He identifies new token-based denial-of-service attack vectors where manipulating token inputs and requested output can jam up model servers, and recommends anomaly detection on model input parameters. He also notes PII/PHI leaking into prompts is a behavioral event security teams should monitor.

sections.title: Q&A: Agent Security and Human-in-the-Loop
sections.summary: Daniel addresses whether agents and human-in-the-loop systems introduce additional security challenges. He references the LLM Top 10 vulnerability list, highlighting excessive agency as a key risk for agents. He gives an example of an assistant changing computer settings requiring admin permissions, where hallucination could cause unmanaged changes. Mitigations include restricting permissions and using a dry-run approach where the agent generates proposed actions (e.g., network configurations) that are then reviewed, approved, or modified by a skilled human before execution. He notes generating the initial set is the hard part while post-editing is relatively easy for skilled engineers.

demonstrations: Customer application assisting field medics in disaster relief and military situations used to illustrate hallucination stakes
Prompt injection firewall with configurable thresholds and individual model calls for pre-production testing
Dry-run agent approach for network configuration updates as an example of human-in-the-loop approval pattern
limitations: RAG grounds output but does not indicate when the model has failed versus succeeded
Data scientists often lack expertise in running microservices at scale and distributed systems
Talk scoped to open-access LLMs; cannot comment on closed systems' risk handling
PII filtering alone is insufficient because prompts may still be logged or stored unencrypted in memory
Database RBAC alone does not fully solve the data access problem for big file stores and data lakes
Agents with excessive permissions can cause unmanaged changes to systems when hallucination occurs
quantitativeClaims: Field medics may deal with 16 different casualties in one case
Daniel has more than ten years of experience developing and deploying ML models at scale
Typical LLM call takes around 4 seconds while smaller NLP models take around 200 milliseconds
